entities.name: Marcus Herennius Picens
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Herennius Picens was a Roman senator who served as suffect consul in 34 BC, replacing Gaius Memmius and occupying the office from November 1 to the end of December. This marked a pivotal moment in the tumultuous years following the death of Augustus, as the Roman Senate struggled to assert its authority amidst the growing power of the imperial system. Picens' tenure was part of a broader effort by the Senate to maintain control over the imperial administration and limit the influence of the Praetorian Guard. However, his time in office was short-lived, and he was ultimately succeeded by the more powerful Claudius, who would go on to play a significant role in shaping the Roman Empire's future. The legacy of Marcus Herennius Picens lies in his attempts to resist the encroachment of imperial power, even as the Roman Senate itself was slowly being eroded by the very system it sought to control.

Picens' appointment was also notable for its association with the complex web of alliances and rivalries that characterized the late Republic. His replacement, Claudius, would form a crucial alliance with the Emperor Tiberius, setting the stage for a period of relative stability and growth under the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Meanwhile, Picens' own family would become embroiled in the intrigue-ridden world of Roman politics, with his son and grandson rising to prominence in their own right.

Despite the significance of Picens' tenure, his name has largely faded from historical memory, lost to the sands of time in a cloud of obscurity. However, for those who seek to understand the intricacies of Roman politics and the machinations of the late Republic, Marcus Herennius Picens remains a fascinating, if lesser-known, figure.
